newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD worried but powerless on S.Korean strife.
newsitem.headline: OECD worried but powerless on S.Korean strife.

text.p: The OECD said on Friday nothing in the international free-market orgnisation's rules allowed it to fault new member South Korea over a crackdown on strikers but it was very concerned by the strife in Seoul.

Secretary General Donald Johnston told a press lunch he had voiced the worries of OECD members last week and could not comment further before a delegation arrived in Paris from Seoul next Tuesday to explain South Korea's position.

Four world labour leaders including OECD adviser John Evans, who should be present at Tuesday's meeting, were hustled out of South Korea on Thursday under deportation threat after attending labour rallies and visiting strike leaders holed up in Myongdong Cathedral in Seoul to avoid arrest.

Deputy Secretary General Joanna Shelton said the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development, of which South Korea became a member in December, was upset by the situation, but she refrained from overt criticism.
Even if the 29-country OECD was attached to protection of human rights, including labour rights, there was nothing in its rules to ensure their respect, beyond peer pressure, she said.
"It was one of the issue raised during the (membership) talks," Shelton told reporters at the lunch. "But there is nothing in the rules."

The labour strife and crackdown on union leaders follows the adoption of laws allowing companies to lay off staff, replace stikers and implement flexible working hours, measures which the government says are needed to cut industrial costs and increase competitiveness.
International labour organisations are pressuring Seoul to abandon the law, which they maintain curbs worker rights to freedom of association.

Shelton's remarks tallied with those of South Korean Labour Ministry official Shim Kyung-Ho, who is due to visit Paris. "All the OECD can do is put peer pressure on us. Nothing more, nothing less," he said in Seoul.
Johnston's statement last week was clearly designed to do just that. "OECD members voiced concerns during Korea's accession process with industrial relations in Korea," it said.
"The Korean government undertook to reform its legislation in line with international standards, including such basic rights as freedom of association and collective bargaining."
